section.title: Healing at Bethesda and the Authority of the Son
section.sectionRationale: The third sign, a man healed at the pool of Bethesda after thirty-eight years, sparks the Gospel's first open conflict. Because Jesus healed on the Sabbath and called God His own Father, making Himself equal with God, the authorities seek to kill Him. Jesus responds with a sweeping discourse on His unity with the Father: the Son gives life and executes judgment, and a chorus of witnesses, John, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures, testify that He is sent from God.
section.thesis: The Son does only what He sees the Father doing, and the Father has granted Him to give life to the dead and to execute all judgment, so that all must honor the Son as they honor the Father, and a fourfold witness, John, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures, confirms that to refuse the Son is to refuse life itself.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the healing at Bethesda and the Sabbath conflict; the discourse on the Son's authority to give life and to judge in perfect union with the Father; and the fourfold testimony, John, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures, that indicts unbelief.

units.label: The pool of Bethesda
units.note: do you want to get well

verses.text: Some time later there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now there is in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate a pool with five covered colonnades, which in Hebrew is called Bethesda.
On these walkways lay a great number of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the paralyzed.
One man there had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.
When Jesus saw him lying there and realized that he had spent a long time in this condition, He asked him, “Do you want to get well?”
“Sir,” the invalid replied, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred. While I am on my way, someone else goes in before me.”
Then Jesus told him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.”
Immediately the man was made well, and he picked up his mat and began to walk. Now this happened on the Sabbath day,
so the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “This is the Sabbath! It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.”
But he answered, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’”
“Who is this man who told you to pick it up and walk?” they asked.
But the man who was healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there.
Afterward, Jesus found the man at the temple and said to him, “See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.”
And the man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.

units.label: The Father and the Son
units.note: the Son gives life and executes judgment

verses.text: Now because Jesus was doing these things on the Sabbath, the Jews began to persecute Him.
But Jesus answered them, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.”
Because of this, the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him. Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.
So Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does.
The Father loves the Son and shows Him all He does. And to your amazement, He will show Him even greater works than these.
For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives {{zoe|life}} to whom He wishes.
Furthermore, the Father judges no one, but has assigned all {{krisis|judgment}} to the Son,
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him.
Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.
Truly, truly, I tell you, the hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.
For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself.
And He has given Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man.
Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice
and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.
I can do nothing by Myself; I judge only as I hear. And My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me.

units.label: Testimonies about Jesus
units.note: John, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures

verses.text: If I testify about Myself, My {{martyria|testimony}} is not valid.
There is another who testifies about Me, and I know that His testimony about Me is valid.
You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth.
Even though I do not accept human testimony, I say these things so that you may be saved.
John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and you were willing for a season to bask in his light.
But I have testimony more substantial than that of John. For the {{ergon|works}} that the Father has given Me to accomplish, the very works I am doing, testify about Me that the Father has sent Me.
And the Father who sent Me has Himself testified about Me. You have never heard His voice nor seen His form,
nor does His word abide in you, because you do not believe the One He sent.
You pore over the Scriptures because you presume that by them you possess eternal life. These are the very words that testify about Me,
yet you refuse to come to Me to have life.
I do not accept glory from men,
but I know you, that you do not have the love of God within you.
I have come in My Father’s name, and you have not received Me; but if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him.
How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?
Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.
If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me.
But since you do not believe what he wrote, how will you believe what I say?”

zoe.gloss: Life, and in John especially the life of God, eternal life. The Father has life in Himself and has granted the Son to have life in Himself, so that the Son gives life to whom He wishes. This life is received now by hearing Christ's word and believing, a crossing over from death to life, and it will be consummated in the resurrection of the body.

krisis.gloss: Judgment, the act of judging and the verdict it renders. The Father has assigned all judgment to the Son, giving Him authority to judge because He is the Son of Man. Judgment is both present, as people respond to His word, and future, at the resurrection to life or to judgment. To honor or dishonor the Son is to settle one's standing before the Judge of all.

martyria.gloss: Testimony, witness, legal evidence. Jesus does not stand on His own unsupported word but marshals a fourfold witness: John the Baptist, the works the Father gave Him to do, the Father Himself, and the Scriptures. In a case where two or three witnesses establish a matter, the testimony to Jesus is overwhelming, so unbelief is shown to be culpable, not reasonable.

ergon.gloss: Work, deed. The Father is always working, even on the Sabbath, and the Son works with Him. The works the Father gave Jesus to accomplish, the signs and ultimately the cross, are themselves a testimony that the Father has sent Him. In John the works reveal the worker; to see the works rightly is to recognize the Son.

basic.context: At a feast in Jerusalem, Jesus heals a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, telling him to pick up his mat and walk. Because it was the Sabbath, the authorities object, and when they learn Jesus did it, and hear Him call God His own Father, they seek to kill Him for making Himself equal with God. Jesus does not soften the claim; He explains it. The Son does only what He sees the Father doing, and the Father has given Him to give life to the dead and to judge all people. He then calls four witnesses to back His claim: John the Baptist, His works, the Father, and the Scriptures.
basic.hermeneutics: The key issue is the identity of Jesus. His enemies rightly understood that calling God His own Father meant claiming equality with God; the question is whether the claim is true. Jesus answers not by retreating but by describing a unique unity with the Father, in work, in giving life, and in judgment. The key questions are, does the Son truly share the Father's authority, and will we honor Him accordingly. The chapter warns that even diligent Bible study is worthless if it does not lead us to come to Christ for life.
basic.originalLanguages: The discourse gathers key words. The Son gives zoe, the very life of God, to whom He wishes. The Father has assigned all krisis, judgment, to the Son. Jesus grounds His claim in a fourfold martyria, testimony: John, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures. And the ergon, the works the Father gave Him, themselves testify that the Father has sent Him.
basic.typology: The Sabbath itself points forward: the Father works to sustain and save even on the Sabbath, and the Son brings the true rest of restored life. Moses, whom the leaders trust, wrote about Christ, so the Scriptures are a signpost to Him. The resurrection to life fulfills the hope of Daniel 12.
basic.christ: Christ claims to share the Father's very life and authority: He gives life to the dead and judges all people. He is to be honored exactly as the Father is honored. He is the Son of Man to whom judgment is entrusted, and the one to whom all the Scriptures point.
basic.god: God is the Father who is always working, who loves the Son and shows Him all He does, and who has given the Son to give life and to judge, so that the Father is honored in the Son. The Father Himself testifies to the Son, and refusing the Son dishonors the Father.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 12 speaks of resurrection to life and to shame. Deuteronomy 19 requires two or three witnesses. Luke 24 shows Christ opening the Scriptures that testify about Him. John 1 said the Word was God, now claimed openly.
basic.oneStory: The one who heals a lifelong invalid claims to share the Father's authority to give life and to judge. The Scriptures the leaders revere, and Moses in whom they hope, all point to Him. The story of God's saving work narrows to the Son who gives life to the dead and before whom all will finally stand.

context.literary:
John 5 is built like a trial. The vocabulary of the courtroom runs through it: testimony, judgment, witnesses, and in verse 45 an accuser. The chapter opens with Jesus as the defendant, charged in verse 16 with Sabbath breaking and in verse 18 with blasphemy, and it ends with the defendants cross examined and the charge turned back on the prosecutors. The same Greek root for 'testify' that carries the whole second half is a legal term, and by verse 45 the court has changed places.

The opening scene, verses 1 to 15, has three small movements: the question and command at the pool, the interrogation by the authorities, and a second meeting at the temple. Notice that the authorities never ask the man who healed him. They ask who told him to carry the mat, verse 12, which shows what they were looking for. Verse 16 is the hinge, turning a healing story into a theological contest.

The first speech, verses 19 to 30, is held together by an inclusio. It begins, 'the Son can do nothing by Himself,' verse 19, and ends, 'I can do nothing by Myself,' verse 30. Inside that frame Jesus names two works that belong to God alone, giving life and judging, and he treats each twice, first as a present reality in verses 21 to 24 and then as a future one in verses 25 to 29. Verse 24 stands at the centre as the offer: hear, believe, and cross from death to life.

The second speech, verses 31 to 47, calls its witnesses in order: John, verses 33 to 35, the works, verse 36, the Father, verses 37 and 38, and the Scriptures, verses 39 to 47. Each is introduced by a short statement and followed by a rebuke, and the final witness is the most severe because it is the one the hearers trust most. Chapter 5 also follows the pattern John uses throughout the Book of Signs: a sign, a misunderstanding, a discourse. The sign this time is deliberately small and private, so that all the weight falls on the argument it provokes.
context.historical:
The pool lay beside the Sheep Gate, a gate that Nehemiah 3:1 says the priests rebuilt, on the north side of the temple area, so the sick lay within sight of the sacrifices they could not take part in. Many ancient copies of verse 3 add that the sick were waiting for a stirring of the water, and a further verse about an angel troubling the pool. The earliest manuscripts do not have it, which is why the BSB jumps from verse 3 to verse 5, but the man's own words in verse 7 show that some such belief was current among the sick.

Thirty-eight years is a long time. Deuteronomy 2:14 uses the same figure for the time Israel spent from Kadesh-barnea until the Brook of Zered, a whole generation lost in the wilderness. John does not point this out, so it is best treated as a possible echo rather than a claim, but a first century hearer steeped in the Torah may well have heard it.

The Sabbath was one of the clearest marks of Jewish identity. The Torah forbids work on that day, Exodus 20:8 to 11, and the prophets applied the ban to carrying loads, Jeremiah 17:21 and 22, a rule Nehemiah enforced at the gates of Jerusalem, Nehemiah 13:19. Later rabbinic collections such as the Mishnah list carrying between private and public space among the forbidden kinds of work, which is the world behind the officials' complaint. The penalty for deliberate Sabbath breaking was death, Numbers 15:32 to 36, so the charge in verse 16 was serious.

Their reaction to verse 17 is just as intelligible. A strict monotheist could say that God keeps ruling and judging on the Sabbath, since birth and death do not stop on the seventh day. To say 'My Father' of God in that exclusive way, and then to claim the same freedom to work, was to put oneself on God's side of the line. That is why the opposition moves at once from rule keeping to a death sentence.
context.canonical:
The discourse gathers three Old Testament themes and carries each to its end. First, God as the one who both kills and gives life. 'I bring death and I give life,' Deuteronomy 32:39, and 'Am I God, killing and giving life?' 2 Kings 5:7, show that the right to raise the dead was taken as the clearest mark of deity. When Jesus says the Son gives life 'to whom He wishes,' he claims that mark for himself. Paul describes the Father the same way, 'the God who gives life to the dead,' Romans 4:17, and says of the last Adam that he became 'a life-giving spirit,' 1 Corinthians 15:45.

Second, the Son of Man. Verse 27 gives the reason the judging is his: 'because He is the Son of Man.' The Greek has no article here, which matches the figure of Daniel 7:13 and 14, 'One like the Son of Man,' who receives 'dominion, glory, and kingship.' Verses 28 and 29 then draw on Daniel 12:2, where many awake 'some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.' The theme reappears when Paul tells the Athenians that God will judge the world 'by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31, and when he says all must appear before 'the judgment seat of Christ,' 2 Corinthians 5:10. Revelation 20:12 shows the books open and the dead standing before the throne.

Third, the Scriptures as witness. John 5:39 and 46 give the principle that Luke 24:27 and 44 carry out, and Acts 10:43 states: 'All the prophets testify about Him.' The Sabbath, finally, is gathered into Christ in the later books: 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9. The sign at Bethesda looks forward to John 11, where the loud voice of verse 25 is heard in front of a tomb, 'Lazarus, come out!' John 11:43.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants his readers to see that the argument about the Sabbath was never really about the Sabbath. He tells the healing briefly and leaves the man oddly unresolved, so that the reader's attention moves to the question the authorities have blurted out: who is this, and by what right? He then lets Jesus answer in the longest unbroken speech so far, and the answer is built to leave no neutral ground. The Son shares the Father's work, the Father's life and the Father's judgment, and so the honour due to the Father is due to the Son.

The speech is also an appeal, not only a defence. Verse 34 says why Jesus is speaking: 'so that you may be saved.' The warning in verses 39 to 47 is aimed at people who were devoted to Scripture, and John means his readers, many of them Jewish believers who had been pressed to prove their new faith from the old books, to hear that Moses and the prophets lead to Christ. Verse 24 is the offer held out in the middle of the trial, and John 20:31 shows what he hopes will happen when it is read: that the reader will believe and have life in his name.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this chapter is description. The pool, the crowd of sick people, the mat and the Sabbath rule belong to one day in Jerusalem, and nothing here commands believers to expect a healing at a particular pool or to treat every unwell person as in the same position as the man of verse 5. Jesus' warning in verse 14, 'Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you,' should not be turned into a rule that every illness is a punishment; John 9:3 shows He denied that link in another case, and this verse speaks to one man.

What the chapter does prescribe is what Jesus says about himself. The honour due to the Father is due to the Son, verse 23. Life comes by hearing and believing, verse 24. The Scriptures are to be searched as witnesses to Christ, verse 39, not worshipped as a possession. The Sabbath question is handled in the same way: the chapter does not abolish rest, but it shows that the Lord of the day acts on it with the Father's authority, and the New Testament goes on to speak of a rest that his people enter, Hebrews 4:9 and 10.

debates.question: Is the Son subordinate to the Father in these verses?

views.label: A subordination of being
views.case: Verses 19, 26 and 30 say the Son can do nothing by himself and receives life from the Father, and Arius and later groups used such lines to say the Son is a lesser, created being.

views.label: An order of relation within one divine life
views.case: The church's reading, from the fourth century, is that the Son's dependence is the dependence of a Son, not of a creature. The same verses say he does 'whatever the Father does,' verse 19, has 'life in Himself,' verse 26, and is to be honoured as the Father is honoured, verse 23. The authorities heard 'equal with God,' verse 18, and the narrator does not correct them.

views.label: A subordination of the incarnate mission
views.case: Some stress that the language belongs to the Son sent into the world, who speaks as one who has taken on the human role of obedience, Philippians 2:6 to 8, while his eternal dignity is not in question.

debates.bearing: All three can be held with the verses, and the second and third are not rivals. The chapter claims the Father's works and honour for the Son in the same breath as his obedience, so that dependence and equality describe one relationship, not competing ones.

debates.question: How should 'You pore over the Scriptures' in verse 39 be read?

views.label: A statement of fact
views.case: The Greek verb can be read as a statement or a command. The BSB and many commentators take it as a statement, since the next words say 'you presume that by them you possess eternal life.' The charge is that their searching never reaches the one it points to, verse 40.

views.label: A command
views.case: Older English versions read it as 'Search the Scriptures.' On this view Jesus tells them to keep searching because the Scriptures testify to him.

debates.bearing: The two readings come to the same place. Searching is good; searching that stops short of coming to Christ, verse 40, leaves a person without life.

study.originalLanguages:
Several small words in this chapter carry more than English shows. In verse 6 the question 'Do you want to get well?' uses hygies, 'whole' or 'sound,' the root behind our word hygiene. John returns to it in verses 9, 11, 14 and 15, and again in 7:23, where Jesus says he made 'the whole man well on the Sabbath.' The word suggests more than the stopping of a symptom; it is a person restored, which is why the later conversation can turn at once to sin and to the temple.

In verse 18 the charge is that Jesus made himself 'equal with God,' isos to theo. The adjective isos means 'the same in measure,' and a related form stands in Philippians 2:6, 'equality with God,' which Christ 'did not consider ... something to be grasped.' John lets the opponents state the claim so bluntly that no one can say the Gospel is hiding it, and Jesus answers by explaining in what way it is true, not by denying it.

Verse 24 says that the believer 'has crossed over from death to life.' The verb is in the perfect tense, which describes a completed act with a lasting result: the believer has moved, and stands on the other side. The same verb and tense return in 1 John 3:14, 'We know that we have passed from death to life,' where the evidence is love. In verse 21 the Son 'gives life' is one word, zoopoiei, a present tense verb. The same verb appears in 6:63, 'The Spirit gives life,' and in Romans 4:17 of the God who 'gives life to the dead.' John is using one word, always God's, for what Father, Son and Spirit do.

When Jesus describes John the Baptist in verse 35 he calls him a lamp, lychnos, that 'burned and gave light.' A lamp is not the sun, and John 1:8 says the same in another way: 'He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light.' The tense is past, since the crowd's enjoyment of John's light 'for a season' had already faded.

Lastly, 'you pore over' in verse 39 translates eraunate, to search out with care. The verb is the one used in 7:52, where the Pharisees tell Nicodemus, 'Look into it, and you will see that no prophet comes out of Galilee.' In both places careful searching is the very thing that leads people astray, because it is done without the willingness to be taught by the one the text is about. In verse 45 the same people have 'put your hope' in Moses, again in the perfect tense: their hope was set on him and still rests there.

typology.type: The Sabbath and the Father's ceaseless work, Genesis 2:2 and 3
typology.fulfillment: On the seventh day God finished creating and rested, Genesis 2:2 and 3, but He did not stop caring for what He had made. Jesus takes up that thought in verse 17: the Father is at work 'to this very day,' and the Son works with Him. The Sabbath pointed to a rest that would come when the work of restoring a broken world is done, and Jesus gives a taste of it in a healed man. The writer of Hebrews says that 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9. The type falls short in that the day gave rest from labour for a day, while the rest in Christ is a settled peace with God. At the cross He says 'It is finished,' John 19:30, and the work that makes the rest possible is done.

typology.type: The prophet like Moses, Deuteronomy 18:15 to 19
typology.fulfillment: Moses promised that God would raise up 'a prophet like me from among your brothers,' and said 'You must listen to him,' Deuteronomy 18:15. The same passage says God will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to that prophet's words, verse 19. Jesus says that Moses 'wrote about Me,' verse 46, and so claims to be the one Moses promised. In John 6:14 the crowd calls Him 'the Prophet who is to come into the world.' He exceeds Moses by being the Son and not a servant in the household, Hebrews 3:5 and 6, and by speaking with the Father's own authority, not only for the Father. The type falls short because Moses could give the law but could not give life, which is why the same Moses becomes the accuser of those who will not believe.

typology.type: Resurrection to life or judgment, Daniel 12:2 and Ezekiel 37
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel's vision of dry bones, 'I will open your graves and bring you up from them,' Ezekiel 37:12, and Daniel's vision of those who awake 'some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt,' Daniel 12:2, set out the hope of Israel for the dead. In verses 25 to 29 Jesus says that the voice that wakes them is his own, and that the man who gave a raised life to the man at the pool will one day call all out of the graves. The sign foreshadows the raising of Lazarus, John 11:43, and then his own, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The type falls short because the prophets saw it in the distance, while in Christ the resurrection is already at work, verse 25: 'has now come.'

typology.type: The thirty-eight years in the wilderness, Deuteronomy 2:14
typology.fulfillment: The match is possible, not certain, and John does not draw it. If it is meant, it is a remarkable one: an entire generation of Israel wasted away in the wilderness for thirty-eight years because of unbelief, Deuteronomy 2:14, and a man in Jerusalem has spent the same number of years unable to rise. In both cases the word that ends the waiting comes from God, and in both the next step is to move. The escalation is that the Lord who sentenced a generation now gives one man the word 'Get up.' The type falls short in that the wilderness generation never entered the land, while the man at the pool is healed on the spot. Because the link is an inference, it is held loosely.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by showing that two works belong to him which the Old Testament reserves for God alone: giving life and passing judgment. Deuteronomy 32:39 and 2 Kings 5:7 treat both as signs of deity, and verses 21 and 22 hand them to the Son. This is the heart of what the authorities heard in verse 18. The point is that Jesus does not stand beside the Father as a gifted messenger; he stands inside the Father's own work.

The title that closes the argument is 'the Son of Man,' verse 27. It points to Daniel 7:13 and 14, where one like a son of man approaches the Ancient of Days and is given dominion that will never pass away, and it gives the reason the judging is entrusted to him. The judge is one of us. Paul says the same when he tells the Athenians that God will judge by 'the Man He has appointed' and has given proof 'by raising Him from the dead,' Acts 17:31. It is a quiet comfort that the one before whom every person will stand has Himself been tested and seen the world from within it, Hebrews 4:15.

Look too at the pattern of the sign. The command to the man, 'Get up,' uses a verb that the New Testament commonly uses for being raised from the dead, and the healing is a down payment on what verses 25 to 29 promise. It also teaches that the life Christ gives is not at the mercy of the pool. The man had waited for a stirred water and for a helper, verse 7, and found that the one who gives life had come looking for him, verse 6.

Christ is also the point of Scripture. Verses 39 and 46 say that the Scriptures, and Moses in particular, 'testify about Me' and 'wrote about Me.' Luke 24:27 gives the content of that claim: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained what was written about Himself. It is wise to guard against forced allegory here. Some early readers saw the five porches as the five books of Moses, but the text does not say so. The better evidence is the line the chapter itself draws: Deuteronomy 18:15 promises a prophet like Moses, and the Sabbath, the sacrifices and the promises of life all find their meaning in the one who can say 'come to Me to have life,' verse 40.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He does not stop working. Genesis 2:2 and 3 says He rested from His work of creation, and the Pharisees assumed that on the Sabbath God simply held still. Verse 17 rejects that picture. The God of Scripture 'will not grow tired or weary,' Isaiah 40:28, and holds all things together, Hebrews 1:3. Rest, for Him, has never meant absence. This shapes worship: we are not praying into a silence on the seventh day, but to the one who is the keeper of Israel and neither slumbers nor sleeps, Psalm 121:4.

Next, the chapter shows a God whose life is shared. The Father 'loves the Son and shows Him all He does,' verse 20, and has 'granted the Son to have life in Himself,' verse 26. Life in Himself is the mark of God's self-existence, and the verse says that it is the Son's too. The honour due to the Father is due to the Son, verse 23, and the New Testament builds worship on that: 'every knee should bow ... and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father,' Philippians 2:10 and 11. The glory of the Son does not rival the Father's; it completes it. No one who has met the Son has been given a second god.

The chapter also holds mercy and justice together without letting go of either. The Father who gives life is the Father who will judge, and verse 29 says the final division follows deeds, which show whether a person has heard and believed. Yet the speech was given 'so that you may be saved,' verse 34, and the offer of verse 24 lies at its centre. God does not take pleasure in the sentence, but He will not pretend there is none.

A further tension is that life is given 'to whom He wishes,' verse 21, and yet 'you refuse to come to Me,' verse 40. The text does not explain how these fit; it leaves both standing. The Father has also spoken, verse 37, though not in a form anyone could see. At Sinai Israel 'saw no form; there was only a voice,' Deuteronomy 4:12, and now the Father speaks through the Son and the works, because the Son is the one who has made Him known, John 1:18. For worship this means that to refuse the Son is not to take a neutral position toward God. It is to turn from the only way the Father has chosen to be known.

crossReferences.note: God rested on the seventh day from the work of creation. The Pharisees took that to mean He is idle on the Sabbath, and verse 17 says He is not. It shows that the Sabbath rest is a rest from making, not from sustaining and saving what He has made.

The figure of thirty-eight years is the length of Israel's wandering from Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Zered, until that generation had perished. John draws no link, so it is only a possible echo, but a man lame for the same length of time inside the sight of the temple may be meant to recall it.

The prophet tells Jerusalem not to carry a load through its gates on the Sabbath, and this is the ground of the officials' complaint about the mat in verse 10. It shows that their objection had a text behind it, which makes their blindness to the one who made the man whole more telling.

The king of Israel asks 'Am I God, killing and giving life?' when he is asked to cure a man. The question shows that giving life was understood as God's alone, and so Jesus' claim in verse 21 to give life to whom He wishes is a claim to what only God can do.

'I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal.' This is the Old Testament statement of the two powers that verses 21 and 22 give to the Son: to give life and to judge. The Lord says there is no god besides Him, and the Son is placed inside that unique claim.

One like a son of man is given dominion, glory and kingship over every nation. Verse 27 gives as the reason for the Son's authority to judge that He is 'the Son of Man,' and the Greek has no article, matching the phrasing of Daniel's vision. The authority is a royal and universal one.

Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt. Verse 29 follows the same two outcomes. The new thing is the voice that does the waking, which Daniel does not name and Jesus says is His own.

A matter must be established by two or three witnesses. Verse 31 grants the principle, 'My testimony is not valid' alone, and verses 32 to 40 supply the witnesses. John 8:17 and 18 returns to the same rule with the Father as a second witness.

Moses promised a prophet like himself and warned that God would hold accountable anyone who did not listen to him. Verse 46 says Moses 'wrote about Me,' and verse 45 says the same Moses is the accuser. To refuse the one he foretold is to fall under his own warning.

'We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers.' The verb and tense match John 5:24, and the verse shows what the crossing looks like in an ordinary life. The life Jesus gives in verse 24 can be recognised by its fruit.

Jesus says to His opponents that if He is not doing the works of His Father they should not believe Him, but if He is, they should 'believe the works themselves.' This repeats verse 36 and shows that the works are offered as evidence for the mind, and not only as wonders.

There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, and whoever enters it rests from his own work, as God did from His. This takes the question raised by the Sabbath healing and answers it: the Father's work and the Son's work make possible a rest that the day could only point to.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 1 and 2 show a world made by a God who then rested, and Genesis 3 shows that death came into that world through disobedience. From that point the question running through the Bible is whether the God who made life can also restore it. The Old Testament answers by hints: God says 'I bring death and I give life,' Deuteronomy 32:39, the prophets see bones rising, Ezekiel 37:12, and a book of Daniel sees the sleepers awaken, Daniel 12:2. Alongside these hints runs the long story of a people who were given the law and its Sabbath as a gift, and who by Jesus' day had come to hold it as a possession and a line of defence.

This chapter is where the answer is given in the first person. The Father has not left the work of life to a pool, or a priest, or a book. He has put it in the hands of the Son, who gives life and who judges because He is the Son of Man, Daniel 7:13 and 14. The Sabbath that began in creation, Genesis 2:2 and 3, finds its goal in him, since the work He does is the work of renewing the world the Father made. The Scriptures lead to him, Moses wrote about him, and the failure of the people to see it is the sad end of a story that began in a garden where a voice was also doubted.

What the chapter sets up is the rest of John. The raising of Lazarus will show verse 25 in action, John 11:43. The cross will complete the work, John 19:30, and the Spirit will give life, John 6:63. The final judgment that Jesus describes here is the scene Revelation 20:12 paints with its open books and the Book of Life. The Bible's last pages bring together the two outcomes of verse 29: a new creation where the thirsty drink without cost and the dead are no more, Revelation 21:4 to 6, and a final separation from the one who is life.

For a reader in the middle of the story the chapter is an invitation as well as a revelation. The man by the pool had been waiting for a helper and found that the answer to thirty-eight years was a person. The question of verse 40 remains the question of the whole Bible: will you come to Him to have life?

quiz.q: Why did the authorities seek to kill Jesus after the healing at Bethesda?

options.text: Because He healed on the Sabbath and called God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.
options.note: Verse 18 gives both reasons, the Sabbath and the claim to deity.

options.text: Only because He broke the Sabbath by healing.
options.note: The Sabbath was one reason, but the deeper offense was His claim to be equal with God.

options.text: Because He refused to heal anyone else at the pool.
options.note: The issue was not whom He healed but the Sabbath and His claim about the Father.

options.text: Because He told the man to stop sinning.
options.note: His words to the man are not the reason given; the conflict was over the Sabbath and His equality with God.

quiz.q: What authority does Jesus claim to share with the Father?

options.text: To give life to the dead and to execute all judgment.
options.note: Verses 21 to 27 assign both life-giving and judgment to the Son.

options.text: Only the authority to heal the sick.
options.note: Healing is a sign, but Jesus claims far more, to give life and to judge all.

options.text: The authority to give eternal life to those who believe.
options.note: True and central, but it omits the equally emphasized authority to judge all people.

options.text: No real authority of His own, only the power to teach.
options.note: Jesus claims to do whatever the Father does, sharing His authority, not merely to teach.

quiz.q: How should people respond to the Son, according to verse 23?

options.text: They must honor the Son just as they honor the Father.
options.note: Verse 23 makes honoring the Son the measure of honoring the Father.

options.text: They should respect Him as one prophet among many.
options.note: He is to be honored as the Father is honored, far above a prophet.

options.text: They should admire His teaching and good works.
options.note: Admiration falls short of the honor due to the Son, which equals the honor due the Father.

options.text: They should give Him the honor due to the Father who sent Him.
options.note: True and close, but it slightly understates that the Son is honored just as the Father is.

quiz.q: What witnesses does Jesus call to testify that He is sent from God?

options.text: John the Baptist, His works, the Father, and the Scriptures.
options.note: Verses 33 to 39 marshal all four witnesses to Jesus.

options.text: Only John the Baptist.
options.note: John is one witness, but Jesus says his own works are a greater testimony, along with the Father and the Scriptures.

options.text: His works and the Scriptures.
options.note: Both are named, but the list leaves out John the Baptist and the Father's own testimony.

options.text: The crowds who saw the healing.
options.note: Jesus does not appeal to the crowd's testimony; He names John, the works, the Father, and the Scriptures.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say about the Scriptures the leaders study so diligently?

options.text: They testify about Him, yet the leaders refuse to come to Him for life.
options.note: Verses 39 and 40 say the Scriptures point to Christ, but the leaders will not come to Him.

options.text: They are unnecessary now that Jesus has come.
options.note: Jesus affirms the Scriptures; the problem is failing to see that they point to Him.

options.text: They contain eternal life apart from Christ.
options.note: The leaders presumed this, but Jesus says life is found in coming to Him, to whom the Scriptures point.

options.text: They bear witness to Christ, and Moses wrote about Him.
options.note: True, but it omits the sharp indictment that they refuse to come to Him to have life.

questions: Jesus asked the invalid, do you want to get well. Where has a long struggle left you resigned, and how might Jesus be asking whether you truly want His healing?
The Son does only what He sees the Father doing, in perfect unity. How does this picture of the Son and the Father deepen your worship of Jesus?
Jesus said whoever hears His word and believes has already crossed from death to life. Do you rest in that present assurance, or do you live as if life is still uncertain?
The leaders searched the Scriptures yet would not come to Christ for life. How can you keep your Bible reading from becoming an end in itself rather than a way to meet Jesus?
Jesus said they sought glory from one another rather than the glory that comes from God. Whose approval are you living for, and how does that shape your faith?

translationNotes.note: Bethesda; the BSB footnote notes that Hebrew may mean Aramaic, and that some manuscripts read Bethzatha. The pool near the Sheep Gate has been located by archaeologists.

The BSB prints verse 3 and moves directly to verse 5, because the words about an angel stirring the water, traditionally numbered verse 4, are absent from the earliest manuscripts. The BSB footnote records the longer reading; it is a later explanatory addition, not part of the original text.
Authority to execute judgment because He is the Son of Man draws on Daniel 7:13-14, where the Son of Man is given dominion and judgment.
The resurrection of life and the resurrection of judgment; the BSB footnote points to Daniel 12:2, the Old Testament hope of a twofold resurrection.
